summary:
Kemerovo Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which is assessed here through the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025). Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. The note contains no oblast-specific information beyond that national framework.

Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the federal propaganda statute by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and states that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 ruling, with sentences running up to 12 years in prison. The same review documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and counted 257 gay-propaganda penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22.

Enforcement inside Kemerovo Oblast itself has produced prison time. RIA Novosti, citing the Federal Security Service, reported that a person already serving a prison sentence in the region received an additional six-year sentence in February for participating in the "LGBT movement" and "involving" other prisoners in its activities.
tangentialFactors:
The volume of enforcement has risen alongside its severity: penalties for propaganda offences totalled 257 in 2023-24, against 22 in 2021-22, and Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism convictions carrying terms of up to 12 years since the November 2023 designation.

Monitoring extends to online conduct. Of the 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024, most were charged over displaying banned symbols on social media, so private-looking online activity can generate a court record.

The Kemerovo case indicates that the designation is applied inside the penal system, where sentences can be extended for perceived participation or recruitment, including activity with other prisoners.

Foreign governments attach explicit warnings to travel in the country: the US State Department advises against all travel and sets out arrest, short detention and deportation for foreigners caught under the propaganda statute.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same statutes as visitors, plus exposure that visitors do not carry. The UK Home Office note records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement across the country between 2022 and 2024.

Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and legal gender recognition is unavailable, so residents cannot correct documents or obtain gender-affirming medical care through domestic channels.

Article 20.3 administrative offences apply to residents for displaying banned symbols, with 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024, mostly over social media posts.

The constitution offers LGBT+ people no specific legal protections, and same-sex marriage is not recognised, leaving residents without relationship-based rights or an explicit non-discrimination remedy.
outOfScopeNotes:
The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025) carries no Kemerovo Oblast-specific material beyond the national framework; the oblast-level picture here rests on a single reported case.

The February additional sentence reported by RIA Novosti cites the Federal Security Service as its source and gives no court name, defendant identity or offence article; that detail is not independently corroborated in the available inventory.

How the 2023 healthcare ban is applied in practice within Kemerovo Oblast, and whether any facility in the oblast still provides trans-related care, is not sourced in the inventory.

The inventory does not identify whether the 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ enforcement between 2022 and 2024 were charged under administrative or criminal provisions, nor how many were prosecuted in Kemerovo Oblast specifically.
